paragraphs: Principal component analysis finds a lower-dimensional subspace that preserves information for reconstructing data. With a finite sample, its estimated subspace differs from the best one for the underlying distribution. This paper studies the resulting excess reconstruction loss and asks which properties of the data distribution determine that error.

The authors establish a central limit theorem for the estimated subspace’s error, then derive the asymptotic distribution of its excess risk. These results characterize fluctuations as the sample size becomes large. They also provide a finite-sample upper bound that approaches the asymptotic characterization, connecting guarantees for limited data with the large-sample picture.

The analysis rests on the geometry of the space of subspaces, called the Grassmannian. The authors prove a controlled-variation property, generalized self-concordance, for the negative block Rayleigh quotient along certain geometric paths from its minimizer. The stated result applies when maximum rotation is less than π/4. This geometric control underpins the paper’s statistical description of PCA reconstruction error.
neurips-2025-a-geometric-analysis-of-pca.tldr: A geometric analysis connects PCA’s subspace estimation error to asymptotic risk distributions and a matching finite-sample upper bound.

paragraphs: Small input changes can cause neural networks to make incorrect predictions even when those changes are hard to perceive. This paper investigates whether building transformation symmetries into a convolutional network can improve its resistance to such attacks. The approach uses layers whose behavior follows rotations and changes in scale in a structured way.

The authors compare two architectures. One processes ordinary features and symmetry-aware features in parallel before combining them; the other applies equivariant operations in sequence. Their theoretical analysis connects these architectural constraints to reduced model complexity, more controlled gradients, and tighter certified robustness bounds within the CLEVER framework. These connections explain how symmetry can influence sensitivity to input changes.

On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CIFAR-10C, the models improve robustness and generalization under FGSM and PGD attacks without adversarial training. The findings support symmetry-aware architecture as a promising way to improve robustness while avoiding the training procedure used by the predominant defense approach. The empirical claim concerns the evaluated datasets and attacks.
neurips-2025-bridging-symmetry-and-robus.tldr: Rotation- and scale-equivariant layers improve adversarial robustness in the reported evaluations without requiring adversarial training.

paragraphs: Controlling a large network requires agents to handle many interacting components while remaining useful when operating conditions change. GSAC addresses both demands by combining causal representation learning with a shared actor-critic policy trained across multiple environments. Its central idea is to identify the local information that matters for each agent’s dynamics.

Each agent learns a sparse causal mask that identifies a minimal set of influential neighborhood variables. These masks produce compact representations of state and environment factors. The authors use these representations to bound the error introduced when value functions consider only neighborhoods within a specified number of graph hops, providing a principled basis for local computation.

The shared policy conditions its decisions on compact environment factors. In a new environment, a few trajectories are used to estimate those factors and adapt the policy. The paper establishes finite-sample guarantees for causal recovery, actor-critic convergence, and the adaptation gap. Reported results show rapid adaptation and improvements over learning from scratch and conventional adaptation methods, linking local representations to both computational scalability and transfer.
neurips-2025-causality-meets-locality-pr.tldr: GSAC combines local causal representations with a shared adaptive policy to scale network control and transfer across environments.

paragraphs: This paper asks which sequence patterns a particular idealized class of transformers can express. The models use fixed numerical precision, strict future masking, soft attention, and no positional encodings. These restrictions define the scope of the analysis: the result characterizes this model class rather than every transformer-based language model.

The main theorem gives an exact correspondence with a fragment of linear temporal logic containing only the past operator. In practical terms, the authors describe the models’ representational capacity through a precisely specified language for expressing temporal relationships. They also connect that logical fragment to classes from formal language theory, automata theory, and algebra, bringing several mathematical perspectives into one framework.

Experiments examine whether trained transformers generalize to sequence lengths beyond those encountered during training. Models trained on languages within the characterized capacity generalize reliably in the reported tests, whereas those trained on languages outside it consistently fail to do so. This agreement links the theoretical expressivity boundary to observed length generalization under the studied idealization.
neurips-2025-characterizing-the-expressi.tldr: A restricted class of fixed-precision transformers exactly matches a temporal-logic fragment, with experiments supporting the resulting expressivity boundary.

paragraphs: Updating a language model’s knowledge becomes difficult when the new information arrives as ordinary text containing intertwined relationships. Methods designed around structured facts can represent that information ambiguously, and multiple edits can interfere with one another. CAKE addresses these connected problems by pairing a richer knowledge representation with a strategy for separating conflicting updates.

Its representation module converts knowledge into a semantically augmented graph. Structural disambiguation clarifies how information is organized, relational enrichment adds connections, and semantic diversification broadens the encoding. The editing component then uses graph coloring to organize conflicting edits and assigns them to orthogonal parameter subspaces, separating the parts of the model used for those updates.

On the AKEW benchmark, CAKE outperforms existing methods and reports a 15.43% improvement in accuracy for llama3 editing tasks. The result supports treating knowledge extraction and edit interference as a joint problem. The framework’s practical contribution is a route from complex unstructured text to model updates that better preserve the intended knowledge relationships while reducing conflicts between edits.
neurips-2025-conflict-aware-knowledge-ed.tldr: CAKE represents unstructured knowledge as an enriched graph and separates conflicting edits to improve language-model knowledge updates.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding speeds up language generation by asking a smaller model to draft tokens that the original model then verifies. On systems with multiple GPUs, the smaller model often benefits from fewer devices than the original model, leaving hardware idle during drafting. EasySpec targets this imbalance by changing how the draft model’s layers execute.

The method breaks dependencies between draft-model layers so that multiple layers can run simultaneously across devices. This produces approximate, or fuzzy, drafts. After each drafting and verification cycle, a single forward pass recalibrates the draft model’s key-value cache, preventing approximation errors from accumulating over time. The method requires no training and can be added to an existing decoding setup.

Evaluations use several open-source language models with smaller models from the same families as drafters. EasySpec reaches a peak speedup of 4.17 times over ordinary decoding while preserving the base model’s output distribution. Drafting accelerates by up to 1.62 times, with a maximum reported speculation-accuracy drop of 7%. These results show how faster approximate drafting can improve overall generation without changing the verified distribution.
neurips-2025-easyspec-layer-parallel-spe.tldr: EasySpec runs draft-model layers in parallel to accelerate speculative decoding while preserving the original language model’s output distribution.

paragraphs: Randomized experiments provide evidence about intervention effects, but collecting enough observations for precise estimates can be expensive. Foundation models can predict experimental responses cheaply, yet inaccurate predictions can undermine statistical conclusions. This paper develops an estimator that combines predictions from multiple foundation models with actual experimental observations while retaining valid inference.

The theoretical contribution is that the estimator remains consistent and asymptotically normal even when model predictions are arbitrarily biased. Its asymptotic variance is no greater than that of the standard estimator using experimental data alone. These are large-sample guarantees: they establish that integrating predictions need not sacrifice the estimator’s limiting statistical properties, even when the predictive models are systematically wrong.

Across several randomized experiments, the combined estimator achieves substantial precision improvements. The largest reported gain corresponds to needing up to 20% fewer observations to match the standard estimator’s precision. The approach therefore uses foundation models to make experimental evidence more informative while keeping real randomized data central to the validity of the conclusions.
neurips-2025-efficient-randomized-experi.tldr: Combining foundation-model predictions with randomized data improves precision while preserving asymptotic validity even with arbitrarily biased predictions.

paragraphs: Very large remote-sensing images contain useful detail, but they create two obstacles for multimodal models: scarce high-resolution training examples and too many visual tokens to process efficiently. GeoLLaVA-8K tackles both through new vision-language datasets and methods for retaining informative image content while reducing the representation’s memory requirements.

The paper introduces SuperRS-VQA and HighRS-VQA, covering 22 dialogue tasks with average image sizes of 8,376 by 8,376 and 2,000 by 1,912 pixels, respectively. Pilot studies find that important information often lies in a small subset of tokens associated with objects. Removing background tokens, such as those representing ocean or forest, can even improve performance in these studies.

Building on that observation, Background Token Pruning and Anchored Token Selection reduce token volume while preserving key semantics. Integrated into the LLaVA framework, these techniques enable GeoLLaVA-8K to handle images up to 8K by 8K resolution. Training on the new datasets yields a reported state-of-the-art result on XLRS-Bench, supporting selective processing as a way to make large remote-sensing inputs manageable.
neurips-2025-geollava-8k-scaling-remote-.tldr: GeoLLaVA-8K combines high-resolution remote-sensing datasets with selective visual-token processing to support images up to 8K by 8K.

paragraphs: Sensory inference involves estimating hidden causes from receptor signals. Those causes often have prior relationships, but representing their correlations can require connections that are biologically implausible or computationally expensive. This paper proposes a circuit inspired by the olfactory bulb that implements correlated priors without direct interactions between the units representing hidden causes.

The mechanism uses sister cells: neurons that share receptor input but connect differently to local interneurons. Their connections indirectly implement the needed interactions among latent units. In this construction, correlated connectivity corresponds to anticorrelation in the prior, and the reverse also holds. Geometric arguments show how to construct connectivity for a specified prior and bound how many causes the construction can accommodate.

Simulations demonstrate useful inference in noisy environments, and the authors compare the resulting dynamics with experimental observations. They also show that sister-cell activations can reveal the implemented prior under certain assumptions about latent representations. Although motivated by olfaction, the proposed mechanism may inform other biological and artificial sensory systems that must reason efficiently about correlated hidden causes.
neurips-2025-inference-with-correlated-p.tldr: An olfactory-inspired sister-cell circuit implements correlated priors indirectly, enabling inference without direct connections among latent-cause units.

paragraphs: Liquid cooling control must keep computing equipment within suitable thermal conditions while limiting energy use across the wider cooling system. LC-Opt provides a benchmark for studying that coupled problem under changing workloads. It builds on a high-fidelity digital twin of the Frontier supercomputer’s cooling infrastructure, covering equipment from site cooling towers to server blade groups.

The environment uses Modelica models and exposes controls through a Gymnasium interface. Reinforcement-learning agents can adjust supply temperature, liquid flow, cabinet-level valves, and cooling-tower setpoints. Because actions affect both local temperatures and overall energy consumption, the task involves multiple objectives. The environment also supports additional components, including a heat recovery unit.

The paper benchmarks centralized and decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning. It also demonstrates transferring learned policies into decision and regression trees for interpretable control, and explores language-model explanations of control actions through an agentic mesh architecture. Its main contribution is a detailed, customizable evaluation setting that brings thermal control, energy optimization, and operator-facing interpretability into the same research workflow.
neurips-2025-lc-opt-benchmarking-reinfor.tldr: LC-Opt benchmarks liquid-cooling controllers using a detailed digital twin that connects equipment temperatures, system energy use, and interpretable control.

paragraphs: Learning tasks across changing domains requires a model to gain specialized knowledge without losing earlier capabilities or weakening generalization. LEBA approaches this problem by connecting new learning to previous task representations and adapters. Its design combines progressive adaptation across domains with a mechanism for revisiting and integrating historical knowledge.

The adaptation module uses a Schrödinger bridge to transfer between distributions and support stable learning as domains change. A separate knowledge-ensemble strategy uses a diffusion model to revisit representations from past tasks, then dynamically combines historical adapters. Together, these components address both the transition into a new domain and the consolidation of what the model learned before.

To keep the adapter collection compact, LEBA selects adapters based on similarity. Learnable weights align replayed samples with the meaning of the current task, helping historical information contribute appropriately. Experiments across multiple benchmarks report reduced catastrophic forgetting, better generalization, and stronger performance than existing methods. The findings support coordinating domain adaptation, replay, and adapter selection within one continual-learning framework.
neurips-2025-learn-and-ensemble-bridge-a.tldr: LEBA combines bridge-based domain adaptation, diffusion replay, and compact adapter ensembles to reduce forgetting across sequential tasks.

paragraphs: A continuous-control policy may need to represent several distinct good decisions for the same situation. Deterministic actors and single Gaussian distributions have limited ability to express that diversity. More expressive diffusion and amortized actors can represent multiple modes, but their difficult-to-evaluate decision probabilities complicate efforts to balance performance, diversity, and computational efficiency.

The authors place these actors within a common framework and prove that policy gradients can optimize them directly through reparameterization. They then introduce a diversity regularizer based on distances between decisions. Because this regularizer does not explicitly require decision probabilities, it can encourage varied behavior even when those probabilities are intractable.

Experiments study multi-goal achievement and generative reinforcement learning, two settings where diverse decisions are particularly relevant. Results demonstrate advantages for multimodal policies and the proposed method, especially in few-shot robustness. The algorithm also performs competitively on conventional MuJoCo benchmarks. Across the experiments, amortized actors emerge as a promising combination of expressive multimodal behavior and strong performance, supporting their further use as policy models.
neurips-2025-learning-intractable-multim.tldr: Reparameterized policy gradients and distance-based diversity regularization make expressive multimodal actors trainable without explicit decision probabilities.

paragraphs: Predicting a user’s future behavior over several steps requires understanding how actions fit together as a sequence. This paper formulates User Behavior Trajectory Prediction to capture those longer-term preferences. Its motivation is that dependencies across an entire list can be missed by methods that treat sequence items too independently.

The proposed Listwise Preference Diffusion Optimization framework trains a diffusion model to optimize preferences over complete item sequences. It uses a Plackett–Luce supervision signal and derives a tight variational lower bound aligned with listwise ranking likelihoods. This alignment ties the denoising process to structured sequence preferences, addressing the independent-token assumption identified in earlier diffusion approaches.

Evaluation combines Sequential Match, a new metric measuring exact agreement with a behavior trajectory, with perplexity, which assesses probabilistic fidelity. These measurements examine both whether a complete prediction matches and how well the model represents observed behavior probabilistically. On real-world user-behavior benchmarks, LPDO consistently outperforms the evaluated state-of-the-art baselines, supporting whole-sequence preference optimization for multi-step forecasting.
neurips-2025-listwise-preference-diffusi.tldr: LPDO trains diffusion models on preferences over entire action sequences to improve multi-step user-behavior prediction.

paragraphs: Choosing a 3D object for a scene involves more than finding the right category or shape. The object also needs to fit the scene’s spatial arrangement, meaning, and visual style. MetaFind addresses retrieval methods that overlook these constraints by using the surrounding scene to guide searches through large repositories of 3D assets.

The framework jointly represents individual objects, including their appearance, and the layout of the scene. A plug-and-play layout encoder captures spatial relationships together with appearance features. This lets retrieval account for how an asset relates to what is already present, making scene context part of the selection process rather than relying only on general-purpose shape representations.

MetaFind also supports building a scene iteratively: as the scene changes, retrieval results adapt to the updated context. Evaluations across several retrieval tasks report better spatial and stylistic consistency than baseline methods. The contribution is therefore a scene-aware retrieval framework whose selections can remain coordinated with an evolving composition throughout the construction process.
neurips-2025-metafind-scene-aware-3d-ass.tldr: MetaFind retrieves 3D assets using object appearance and scene layout to improve spatial and stylistic consistency.

paragraphs: This paper models sensory input as observations of a high-dimensional stochastic system and proposes that neurons learn groups of stimuli with related temporal behavior. These coherent sets contain states whose trajectories remain cohesive over a finite period. A neuron then assigns new stimuli a membership index based on the temporal structure learned from experience.

The mathematical construction identifies these sets through spectral clustering of the stochastic Koopman operator. For multivariate Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes, the relevant singular function becomes a linear projection onto a particular direction in a whitened transition matrix. Representing that direction as a receptive field lets a neuron determine membership from the projection’s sign, providing a biologically plausible implementation.

The framework distinguishes neurons detecting common futures from those detecting common pasts. Since neurons do not have access to the underlying equations, the required directions can be estimated from observations using past–future canonical correlation analysis, with an extension to nonlinear dynamics. The authors propose this as an account of temporal filtering, response rectification, and neuronal functional divisions, with potential applications to bio-inspired artificial systems.
neurips-2025-neurons-as-detectors-of-coh.tldr: The paper proposes that sensory neurons identify stimulus groups with shared pasts or futures by learning coherent sets in sensory dynamics.

paragraphs: Switching between smartphone cameras during zoom can produce visible jumps because the cameras differ in geometry and image processing. Training interpolation methods to smooth these transitions is difficult when suitable ground-truth data are scarce and moving scenes create ambiguity. OmniZoom addresses both training data and the representation of the transition.

Its virtual data-generation method uses 3D Gaussian Splatting to model spatial transitions while adapting colors to account for photometric differences. Cross-domain consistency learning aligns semantic information across devices. The framework also introduces 3D Trajectory Progress Ratio Mapping, which goes beyond a purely two-dimensional treatment of interpolation. A texture-focused strategy preserves fine detail, while mask penalties suppress artifacts.

The pipeline works with multiple interpolation methods and reports good performance across public benchmarks. Evaluations on several smartphone platforms find significant quality improvements after fine-tuning with its synthetic data. These findings support virtual cross-device training examples and three-dimensional transition modeling as useful components for smoother zoom, with the real-world improvements specifically tied to the reported fine-tuning procedure.
neurips-2025-omnizoom-a-universal-plug-a.tldr: OmniZoom combines synthetic cross-device data and three-dimensional transition modeling to improve smooth zoom between smartphone cameras.

paragraphs: Text-to-image systems need evaluation that reflects more than the overall appearance of their outputs. The paper argues that earlier benchmarks provide incomplete coverage, particularly for rendered text, style, and image generation requiring reasoning. OneIG-Bench is designed to examine these capabilities through a more comprehensive and finely separated evaluation framework.

Its dimensions include alignment with requested subjects and elements, precision of text rendering, reasoning-dependent content, stylization, and diversity. Separating these dimensions helps reveal where a model succeeds and where it encounters difficulties. A model’s ability to create attractive imagery can therefore be assessed alongside its handling of the specific content and constraints expressed in a prompt.

The contribution is an evaluation resource for analyzing strengths and bottlenecks across image generation. Its structured coverage supports more detailed comparisons between models and helps researchers investigate capabilities that older evaluation systems did not adequately address. The authors make the code and dataset publicly available to support reproducible studies and cross-model comparisons; the abstract does not announce a winning model.
neurips-2025-oneig-bench-omni-dimensiona.tldr: OneIG-Bench evaluates image generators across content alignment, text rendering, reasoning, style, and diversity.

paragraphs: OpenOmni addresses the difficulty of building open-source models that connect images, text, and speech while producing expressive speech quickly. Its two-stage training process separates multimodal alignment from speech generation, targeting both limited training data and the challenge of real-time emotional output.

During alignment, a pretrained speech model receives further training on image-text tasks. The authors report near-zero-shot transfer from vision to speech and stronger performance than models trained on tri-modal data. During speech generation training, a lightweight decoder learns from speech tasks using direct preference optimization, enabling high-fidelity output with emotional expression.

The reported model exceeds state-of-the-art results across omnimodal, vision-language, and speech-language benchmarks. On OmniBench, it improves by four absolute points over VITA while using five times fewer training examples and a smaller model configuration. In non-autoregressive mode, speech latency is below one second and inference is five times faster than autoregressive methods. Emotion-classification accuracy improves by 7.7%. Together, these findings connect progressive alignment with data efficiency and the decoder’s design with faster expressive speech.
neurips-2025-openomni-advancing-open-sou.tldr: OpenOmni uses progressive multimodal alignment and preference-trained speech generation to improve cross-modal performance and deliver real-time emotional speech.

paragraphs: Learning a directed acyclic graph of causal relationships is difficult when data are noisy or limited. Prior knowledge can help, but it may describe relationships less precisely than the numerical edge weights used by a learning method. This paper investigates how that mismatch can distort weights and lead to substantial errors in the learned graph.

The authors analyze the effect of edge-weight deviations during optimization. They identify two graph patterns associated with these deviations and show that the patterns become more common as deviation increases. These patterns provide observable structural signals of a problem originating in how prior knowledge interacts with the numerical learning process.

The Pattern-Guided Adaptive Prior framework uses those signals while learning. It detects the identified patterns and adjusts the structure-learning process to counteract weight deviation, making prior integration adaptive. Experiments support the method’s effectiveness and robustness. The contribution is a connection between a theoretical source of error, its visible consequences in graph structure, and a mechanism for responding during optimization.
neurips-2025-pattern-guided-adaptive-pri.tldr: PGAP detects graph patterns caused by mismatched prior information and adaptively adjusts causal structure learning to reduce the resulting errors.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks are attractive for low-power control on neuromorphic hardware, but continuous-control reinforcement learning commonly relies on mechanisms developed for conventional neural networks. This paper identifies a mismatch between gradual target-network updates and the discrete, non-differentiable dynamics of spiking neurons. The authors show that this mismatch destabilizes training and reduces performance.

Their proxy target framework introduces a network with continuous, differentiable dynamics to support smooth target updates. This changes the training machinery while keeping deployment centered on the spiking network. Because the proxy is used only during training, it adds no inference overhead to the deployed controller.

Across continuous-control benchmarks and several spiking-neuron models, the method consistently improves training stability and achieves performance gains of up to 32%. The authors also report that networks using simple Leaky Integrate and Fire neurons surpass conventional neural-network counterparts, describing this as a first to their knowledge. The findings show why adapting reinforcement-learning algorithms to spiking dynamics can matter for combining control performance with efficient deployment.
neurips-2025-proxy-target-bridging-the-g.tldr: A continuous proxy target stabilizes reinforcement learning for spiking controllers without adding deployment overhead.

paragraphs: Rooms from Motion treats indoor object detection as a combined camera-localization and mapping problem. It starts from images without known camera poses and represents scene geometry through oriented 3D object boxes. This lets the method build a semantic scene map while also estimating where the cameras were when the images were captured.

The key change is replacing a conventional structure-from-motion matcher based on 2D keypoints with an object-based matcher using 3D boxes derived from images. Matching these boxes yields metric camera poses and object tracks, which support construction of a global map. When camera poses are already available, optimizing global boxes against individual observations further improves map quality.

On CA-1M and ScanNet++, the method reports strong localization and higher-quality maps than leading point-based and multi-view object-detection methods. Its representation remains sparse because mapping complexity is proportional to the number of objects. The result extends object-level box representations to complete scenes while bringing localization and semantic mapping into a shared geometric framework.
neurips-2025-rooms-from-motion-un-posed-.tldr: Rooms from Motion matches image-derived 3D object boxes to jointly estimate camera poses and build sparse semantic scene maps.

paragraphs: Larger language models often have lower loss, following regular scaling patterns whose origins remain debated. This paper studies representation superposition as a contributor: a model stores more features than it has representational dimensions, so feature directions overlap. The authors investigate how this overlap affects loss as model dimension changes.

Using a toy model, they control the degree of superposition through weight decay. With weak superposition, loss follows a power law only when feature frequencies themselves follow a power-law distribution. With strong superposition, loss scales inversely with model dimension across a broad class of frequency distributions. The explanation centers on geometric overlap between representation vectors.

The authors report that examined open-source language models operate in the strong-superposition regime and exhibit inverse-dimension loss scaling. They also find the Chinchilla scaling laws consistent with this behavior. These results support superposition as a central contributor to scaling, connecting an internal representational mechanism to observed performance trends and informing when those trends might improve or break down.
neurips-2025-superposition-yields-robust.tldr: The paper links strong representation superposition to inverse-dimension loss scaling across a broad class of feature-frequency distributions.

paragraphs: Extended reasoning can improve a language model’s answers, but it also consumes tokens and increases response time. For simple queries, that extra computation may be unnecessary. This paper introduces hybrid-reasoning models that use query context to decide whether to engage in an extended reasoning process before producing an answer.

Training has two stages. Hybrid Fine-Tuning provides an initial foundation for the two modes, followed by online reinforcement learning using Hybrid Group Policy Optimization. Through this process, the model implicitly learns to select an appropriate reasoning mode. The paper also introduces Hybrid Accuracy to evaluate the model’s ability to perform hybrid reasoning.

Experiments report adaptive behavior across queries of different types and difficulty levels. The models outperform the compared reasoning models and conventional language models in reasoning and general capabilities while improving efficiency. These findings support learning when to reason as part of model training itself. The intended benefit is to retain the value of extended reasoning while avoiding its token and latency costs on queries where it is unnecessary.
neurips-2025-think-only-when-you-need-wi.tldr: Hybrid-reasoning models learn when to use extended reasoning, improving reported capabilities while reducing unnecessary computation.

paragraphs: Reward models help align vision systems with human preferences, so inaccurate judgments can provide misleading training signals. UnifiedReward-Think investigates whether longer, explicit reasoning improves those judgments. It supports both visual understanding and image-generation evaluation, using step-by-step reasoning across multiple dimensions of a response or output.

Training begins with a small amount of image-generation preference data used to distill GPT-4o’s reasoning format. The model then reasons over a larger collection of multimodal preference data spanning vision tasks. Correct reasoning outputs are retained for rejection-sampling refinement, while incorrectly predicted examples feed a reinforcement-learning stage using Group Relative Policy Optimization. This stage encourages exploration of alternative reasoning paths.

Experiments find that incorporating long reasoning chains significantly improves reward-signal accuracy. After this training, the model also exceeds existing baselines when giving answers without explicit reasoning traces. The findings support both the immediate value of explicit reasoning for evaluation and the possibility that learning to reason can improve later direct judgments. The framework thus connects reasoning-focused training with more accurate multimodal feedback.
neurips-2025-unified-multimodal-chain-of.tldr: UnifiedReward-Think improves multimodal reward accuracy through reasoning-focused training and retains gains even without explicit reasoning traces.

paragraphs: This paper develops a framework that interleaves image generation and image understanding within a unified reasoning process. Its motivation is that incomplete integration between these abilities limits self-reflection and reasoning across modalities. Connecting them more directly gives the model a way to combine producing visual content with understanding that content during generation.

The training process starts with a small amount of multimodal chain-of-thought data, then uses reinforcement learning to guide the integration of generation and understanding. A momentum-based reward function adjusts the reward distribution using historical improvements. This mechanism is designed to maintain stability across multiple generations as the model learns through reinforcement.

Experiments report a 22% improvement over the base model on Geneval when multimodal chain-of-thought is integrated. The authors connect this gain to better image-generation quality and closer adherence to instructions. The contribution is a training framework that combines cross-modal reasoning with a reward mechanism informed by past progress, supporting the reported benefits of reasoning within unified image generation and understanding.
neurips-2025-vinci-deep-thinking-in-text.tldr: Vinci integrates image generation and understanding through multimodal reasoning and reinforcement learning, reporting a 22% gain over its base model on Geneval.
